words.intro: A German parents’ evening takes place on tiny chairs. Thirty adults discuss one school trip for two hours, and then someone asks about the sandwiches. It’s the purest form of German democracy.

grammar[0].fact: Parents in Germany elect their reps, and schools have a *Schulkonferenz* that may include pupils. At about ten, most German children are sorted into different kinds of secondary school. Few things are argued about more.

grammar[1].fact: In Germany marks run from 1 to 6, and *Sitzenbleiben*, repeating a year, is still real in many states. There’s also a *Blauer Brief*, a warning letter, sent to parents when a child is in danger of it. Some states are slowly abolishing all this. Others say it’s the end of civilisation.

document.intro: A real blackboard in a German primary school, with today’s lesson still on it. It’s grammar, and you can read it: *Verschiedene Satzarten*, different kinds of sentences. A dot for a statement, an exclamation mark for an exclamation.
document.fact: Pupils in German primary schools learn the grammar words in German: *Tunwort* or *Verb*, *Namenwort* or *Nomen*, *Wiewort* for an adjective. So at parents’ evening, you may find the eight-year-olds know more grammar than their parents.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with the word that belongs to each.
reading.title: Tagesordnungspunkt 7
reading.intro: Parents’ evening, class 4b. Lena has come for her neighbour’s son, as a favour. The school trip, on point seven of the agenda, costs 84 euros, and it has been under discussion since half past seven. It’s now twenty to ten. The chairs are very small.
reading.fact: At a *Klassenfahrt*, teachers take the class away for several days at a stretch, *Elternabend* is a real institution, with an agenda and elected parents’ reps. School in Germany usually starts at about eight, and a child who’s late is noted in the *Klassenbuch*.
